newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers say proposed tobacco rules limit speech.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers say proposed tobacco rules limit speech.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The tobacco industry's challenge to strict new federal limits on cigarette advertising has forged an unusual kinship between manufacturers and media lawyers who believe some of the rules may violate First Amendment rights.

"I think it will be a very tough sell for FDA to persuade courts that its limitations on advertising can be reconciled with the First Amendment," said Floyd Abrams, a prominent free speech lawyer, referring to the Food and Drug Administration, which proposed the rules after getting authorization from President Clinton last year.

Abrams, who helped the tobacco industry with part of its case, said a key problem with the FDA's rules was that while they were designed to protect children, they also would affect adults by limiting ads in many magazines and on billboards.

The situation is ironic on two fronts. Not only have tobacco companies challenged some major news organizations' free speech rights to publicize certain information about cigarettes, but prominent media lawyers see merit in the industry's allegations that the proposed rules would place unconstitutional limits on commercial speech.
"I would not not be surprised if parts of the rules are found to violate the First Amendment," said Michael Bamberger, a free speech expert with the law firm of Sonnenschein Nath & Rosenthal.

"There is always a concern among those of us who spend much of our time worrying about First Amendment that a limitation in one factual context ... will carry over. One really has to look at the First Amendment as a whole and has to be alert," he said.

Clinton authorized the FDA in August 1995 to regulate how cigarettes are sold and marketed in a bid to curb smoking among children. The FDA regulations would ban free samples and billboard ads near schools and playgrounds, limit vending machine sales and ban sponsorship of sporting events and the use of cigarette brands on hats, T-shirts and other products.

The tobacco industry sued the FDA to block enforcement of the new rules. Cigarette companies filed their final written arguments in the case this week. Oral arguments are set to start on Feb. 10 in federal court in Greensboro, N.C.

The industry's suit contains three main challenges to the rules, one of them alleging First Amendment violations. The suit alleges that the proposed advertising limits are excessive and therefore unconstitutional and that the goals can be accomplished through ways that would not limit speech.

"FDA's rules bar far more advertising than any regulatory regime ever approved by any court. Its rules prohibit, or severely circumscribe, almost every method of communicating effectively to adults," the industry said in a brief.
Media lawyers said the rules seemed to violate the First Amendment.

"In this area where the government's interest is said to be that of protecting children, there are obviously other means the government could use, the most obvious being to far more strictly enforce the limitation against the sale of tobacco to underage people," Abrams said.

"If the government did that by increasing criminal penalties and increasing enforcement efforts" they could more directly address the problem "rather than through the peripheral way of limiting advertising," he said.
Bamberger said he thought a government-funded anti-smoking television campaign aimed at children could help reduce smoking.

William Schultz, the FDA's deputy commissioner for policy, said direct action must be taken against tobacco advertising. He said the limitations were not excessive because they were narrowly tailored and did not ban all advertising.
"I think we have a very strong record that the promotion and advertising is a big piece of why kids smoke," he said.

"What advertising does is it creates an appeal, it basically makes this product look very attractive and it's associated with sports and sex and fun and danger and a lot of signals that are appealing to children ... .the effect of that is to induce kids to smoke," Schultz said.
He said limiting access to cigarettes is not enough to stop smoking among children. "They'll get (cigarettes) if they have that desire, so you have to deal with the appeal."
He said commercials and ads aimed at discouraging underage smoking would be insufficient.

"The (tobacco industry's) strategy has been to inundate us with advertising that makes the product seem acceptable, ordinary, more like a common product and it counteracts any sort of message or education about the risks of the product," he said.
A group of advertising associations and the National Association of Convenience Stores have filed separate suits challenging the regulations.
Virginia, Kentucky and North Carolina, all major tobacco-growing states, have filed court papers urging the court to overturn the regulations.
But a far greater number of states -- at least 33 -- along with San Francisco and Guam have asked the court to uphold the rules.
